name: Bolotnik
description: Bolotnik (also known as Bolotny or the Swamp Spirit) is a malevolent entity from Slavic mythology, particularly prevalent in the folklore of Belarus and western Russia, where vast marshlands and peat bogs dominate the landscape. The name derives from 'boloto,' the Russian and Belarusian word for swamp, and the Bolotnik is the embodiment of the dangers that lurk in these treacherous wetlands. Unlike the more neutral water spirits like the Vodyanoy, who rules deeper waters, the Bolotnik is exclusively associated with the shallow, murky bogs and marshes where the ground is unstable and a wrong step can mean a slow, suffocating death. The Bolotnik is believed to be the spirit of someone who drowned in the swamp or who was cursed to guard the marshes for eternity. It is universally feared by villagers living near large wetlands, who tell stories of the Bolotnik's favorite Game: waiting silently just beneath the surface, grabbing the ankles of unwary travelers, and pulling them down into the peat where their bodies are never found. The spirit is particularly active during foggy weather and twilight hours, when visibility is poor and the boundaries between solid ground and treacherous bog are hardest to distinguish
source: Belarusian folklore — Bolotnik swamp spirit documented in Belarusian oral tradition.

name: Bon Bibi
description: Bon Bibi (also written as Bonobibi or Bonbibi) is a revered forest goddess and the primary protective deity of the Sundarbans mangrove forest, the largest tidal mangrove forest in the world, spanning the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers between Bangladesh and India. Bon Bibi is the central figure of a unique syncretic folk religion practiced by the honey collectors, woodcutters, and fishermen who risk their lives daily in the Sundarbans, where the Bengal tiger (known as Dakshin Ray's avatar) claims many lives each year. The name 'Bon Bibi' means 'Lady of the Forest' in Bengali, and she is worshipped by both Hindus and Muslims, representing a rare and beautiful example of religious syncretism in South Asian folk tradition. According to legend, Bon Bibi was sent by Allah to the Sundarbans to protect the faithful from the depredations of the demon king Dakshin Ray, who demanded human sacrifices. She defeated Dakshin Ray and established a truce: she would protect those who entered the forest with respect and pure hearts. Bon Bibi's worship involves no grand temples—only small shrines at the edges of the forest where offerings are left before entering the tiger-infested wilderness
source: Bangladesh mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Boruta
description: Boruta is a powerful forest and swamp spirit from Polish mythology, often considered the Polish equivalent of the Russian Leshy, though with distinct characteristics that reflect the specific landscape and cultural traditions of Poland. Boruta is the tutelary spirit of the forests and marshlands, particularly associated with the vast woodlands of central and eastern Poland, including the legendary Puszcza Kurpiowska and the swamps of Polesie. Unlike the anthropomorphic Leshy, Boruta is often depicted as a nobleman or szlachcic (Polish nobleman) who made a pact with dark forces and was condemned to haunt the forests for eternity. His name is believed to derive from the Old Polish word 'bor' meaning pine forest, connecting him intrinsically to the coniferous woodlands that once covered much of Poland. Boruta is a complex figure—he is not purely evil but rather a trickster and a punisher of those who disrespect the forest. He is known to lead travelers astray, especially those who hunt for sport, log illegally, or pick mushrooms without leaving offerings. However, he can be surprisingly helpful to those who show proper respect for the wilderness, guiding lost children home and protecting the forest from genuine threats
source: Polish folklore — Boruta is a forest spirit documented in Polish oral tradition.

name: Botamochi bakemono
description: Botamochi bakemono is a peculiar and relatively obscure yokai from Japanese folklore, known primarily as an auditory phenomenon that haunts traditional wooden houses. The name 'botamochi' refers to a type of sweet rice cake (botamochi) eaten during the spring equinox, and 'bakemono' means 'transforming thing' or monster in Japanese. According to legend, this mysterious yokai lives beneath the floorboards of old houses, where it engages in its signature activity: mimicking human voices with uncanny accuracy. The Botamochi bakemono is most active during the night, when it imitates the voices of family members to confuse, frighten, and occasionally amuse the household. Unlike more malevolent Japanese yokai such as the oni or yurei, the Botamochi bakemono is considered a relatively harmless prankster, more annoying than dangerous. Its pranks serve as a reminder of the thin boundary between the human world and the spirit world, and its presence in a house was traditionally seen as evidence that the dwelling had a soul of its own. The Botamochi bakemono belongs to the category of 'house yokai' that includes the Zashiki-warashi and the Makura-kashi, spirits that share domestic spaces with humans and interact with them in ways ranging from helpful to mischievous
source: Japanese folklore; a yokai that mimics voices from under floorboards.

name: Bou Saadia
description: Bou Saadia (Father of Saadia) is a tragic folkloric figure from Tunisian tradition, particularly associated with the medina of Tunis and Stambeli ritual performances. According to legend, Bou Saadia came from sub-Saharan Africa in search of his daughter Saadia, who was sold into slavery in Tunis. He is described as a man who went mad with grief, wandering door to door in the medina, humming and dancing, searching for his lost child. His appearance is striking — black skin, leather clothes covered with cowrie shells, and brusque bodily movements that frightened local children. The story reflects Tunisia's history of trans-Saharan slavery, which continued until the early 20th century. No one knows exactly when the legend originated, but Bou Saadia never finds Saadia and is said to continue his eternal search. During Ramadan, he appears in street performances as part of Stambeli rituals (a Tunisian trance-healing tradition with sub-Saharan roots). The legend explores themes of loss, displacement, and the enduring trauma of slavery in Tunisian society
source: Africa is a Country (Maha Abdelhamid); New Lines Magazine; oral Tunisian Stambeli traditions

name: Bouki (Haitian Trickster Hyena)
description: Bouki is the slow-witted, greedy hyena trickster of Haitian folklore -- the eternal foil to the clever Rabbit (or Malis/Connen, the rabbit trickster). In classic Haitian folktales, Bouki is always scheming for an easy meal or some treasure, and he is always outsmarted by the clever rabbit, suffering humiliation or injury. Bouki represents the dangers of greed, gluttony, and stupidity. Unlike the clever Anansi or the sneaky Malis rabbit, Bouki thinks he is cunning but is fundamentally foolish. His name derives from the Wolof word mbouki (hyena) from Senegal, proving his West African origins. Bouki tales were brought to Haiti by enslaved Senegambians and remain a staple of Haitian oral tradition -- they are told in Haitian Creole (Kreyol) and used to teach children moral lessons about generosity, honesty, and the consequences of greed. The name Bouki is a common Creole insult in Haiti, meaning someone foolish or easily tricked
source: Haitian oral tradition, Haiti folklore

name: Bu Draya
description: Bu Draya (also Bu Daryā, meaning 'Father of the Sea' from Persian) is a terrifying sea jinn from Bahraini and Arabian Gulf folklore. Believed to be a malevolent water spirit, Bu Draya appears in the darkest nights to prey on pearl divers and sailors. Described as a huge half-human, half-amphibious creature, it summons winds and controls waters to capsize boats. Its most notorious trick is mimicking drowning cries at night — when a sailor jumps in to rescue what sounds like a comrade, Bu Draya seizes and devours them. According to Bahraini tradition, if sailors recognize Bu Draya aboard their vessel, they must shout for axes and saws (al-jadum wal-minshar), which frightens the creature back into the sea. The legend is intimately tied to Bahrain's pearling heritage, serving as both a cautionary tale and an explanation for the dangers of the sea
source: Folk Culture Bahrain Journal; Pechcin, 'A Tale of the Lord of the Sea'; Gulf Weekly; oral Bahraini traditions

name: Buda
description: Buda (Ge'ez: ቡዳ) is a powerful and feared figure in Eritrean and Ethiopian folk religion, representing the supernatural power of the evil eye combined with the ability to shapeshift into a hyena. The belief is deeply rooted in the highland cultures of Eritrea, particularly among Tigrinya-speaking communities. Buda is believed to be a power held and wielded by specific individuals, often associated with marginalized social groups such as metalworkers (täbbäb), potters, tanners, and weavers. The power is thought to be hereditary, transmitted through family lines, and can be either conscious or unconscious. Those with Buda can harm others through their gaze, causing illness, misfortune, or even death. By night, they are believed to transform into hyenas to attack livestock, desecrate graves, or harm enemies. Protective measures including amulets (kitab), holy water, and invocations of God's name are used to ward against Buda's effects In Eritrea folklore, this figure is known among the Eritrea people.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buda_(folklore) / https://everything.explained.today/Buda_(folklore)/

name: Bunyip
description: Aboriginal Australian water spirit ('bunyip' = devil/spirit) from southeastern Australia (Yorta Yorta, Ngarrindjeru, Wonnarua, Kurnai). Lives in waterholes, billabongs, swamps, rivers. Spiritual Guardian of water - not just monster. The word today means 'devil' but represents deep spiritual significance. Different descriptions: dog-like face, flippers/webbed feet, round head + elongated neck (like diprotodon), body like ox/hippo/manatee. Some say Manatee-like, others emu-neck with folds of skin. First written description 1845: pale blue eggs, deadly claws, brightly colored chest. Makes booming/roaring noises that may be bittern bird. Eats women and children - Warned to avoid deep water. Connected to Dreamtime and sacred waterways. Ngarrindjeri: 'Mulyawonk' - punishes those who take too much fish, takes children who go too close
source: Aboriginal Australian folklore, Dreamtime oral traditions

name: Kinkirsi (Kinkirga)
description: Kinkirsi (singular: Kinkirga) are the powerful nature spirits of the Mossi people of Burkina Faso, invisible beings that inhabit the untamed wilderness beyond village boundaries. According to Mossi cosmology, these spirits are 'as numerous as the stars' and occupy all spaces not inhabited or cultivated by humans — sacred woods, hills, rivers, rocky outcrops, and wild plains. The Kinkirsi are described as small, invisible beings with large heads and long hair, and they play an essential role in human procreation: Mossi tradition holds that a Kinkirga spirit enters a woman's womb during conception, contributing the spiritual essence of the child. Twins (called Kinkirsi themselves) are considered especially sacred as they represent a double spiritual presence. These spirits also claim ownership of wild animals and must be respected by hunters. The Kinkirsi are fundamentally ambiguous — they can be protective ancestors or troublesome tricksters depending on how they are treated. They reproduce an anthropomorphic society in the invisible world, with their own social structures and customs parallel to human Mossi society
source: Mossi oral tradition

name: Mba-Soêmba
description: Mba-Soêmba is the clever hare trickster figure in Mossi folklore of Burkina Faso, the wise and cunning counterpart to the foolish hyena Mba-Katrè. In the vast oral tradition of the Mossi (Moose) people, Mba-Soêmba represents intelligence, quick thinking, and resourcefulness — consistently using his wits to overcome larger, stronger adversaries. Through clever deception, strategic thinking, and an understanding of human nature, the hare repeatedly triumphs over the hyena's brute force and greed. The stories of Mba-Soêmba serve as a cornerstone of Mossi moral education for children aged 10 to 12, teaching that intelligence and patience are more valuable than physical strength. The hare's cunning is celebrated rather than condemned, as his tricks typically punish greed, arrogance, and foolishness. These tales are traditionally performed by griots and elders during evening gatherings, combining entertainment with cultural education. The Mba-Soêmba figure belongs to a broader West African tradition of trickster hares found across the region, from Ghana to Mali
source: Mossi oral tradition

name: Sumbo
description: Sumbo refers to the ritual masks of the Bwaba (Bobo) people of Burkina Faso, which are believed to embody powerful spirits that connect the human world with the invisible realm of ancestors and bush spirits. In Bwaba cosmology, the Sumbo masks represent a complex spiritual system that mediates between two categories of invisible entities: the ancestors and the bush spirits (genies de brousse). The Sumbo tradition includes different types of masks, from the most sacred fresh leaf masks (made from specific species of bush trees and associated with the Do initiatory cult) to fabric masks used in public ceremonies. The leaf masks, made fresh for each ceremony, are considered the most spiritually potent and are intimately connected to the cycle of vegetation. The Do cult, to which the Sumbo masks are linked, is an initiatory society that structures Bwaba social organization into three categories: farmers, blacksmiths, and griots. During ceremonies, the masks serve as the visible manifestation of the spirits, ensuring that proper rituals are observed, ancestors are honored, and the community maintains harmony with the natural and supernatural worlds
source: Bwaba oral tradition and ethnography

name: Imana
description: Imana is the supreme creator deity in the traditional Barundi (and Banyarwanda) religion of Burundi and Rwanda. Unlike the many intervening spirits of the Kubandwa tradition, Imana is seen as the almighty and gracious creator who rules all living things but does not normally interfere in the material course of nature. In Barundi mythology, Imana created the world and humanity, then hunted Death itself as a savage wild animal to grant immortality to creation. During this hunt, Imana commanded all people to stay hidden so Death would have no refuge. However, an old woman disobeyed by creeping out to her vegetable garden, allowing Death to hide under her skirt and enter her home. She died, and when her daughter-in-law—who hated her—filled the cracks in her grave with dirt, she sealed humanity's fate, making death permanent. Imana does not intervene directly in daily affairs, leaving that role to the Imandwa spirits led by Kiranga. This theological distinction—a supreme creator who delegates to lesser mediating spirits—demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of divine hierarchy
source: Wikipedia - Imana; Sacred Texts - Myths and Legends of the Bantu; MexicoHistorico - Burundi Myths

name: Imandwa Spirits
description: The Imandwa are the collective spirits and initiated members of the Kubandwa spirit cult in Burundi and Rwanda, forming a hierarchical pantheon of approximately forty distinct spirits. This spirit pantheon includes Kiranga (Ryangombe) as the supreme leader, his son and successor Binego, other sons like Ruhanga, legendary heroes like the Rwandan prince Kibogo, and various animal and nature spirits. The Imandwa serve as active intermediaries between the supreme creator Imana and human beings, influencing every aspect of life including agriculture, fertility, health, hunting, marital love, and prosperity. Unlike ordinary ghosts (bazimu) who are mostly malevolent, the Imandwa are a superior order of spirits who can be petitioned through proper ritual. The term 'Imandwa' refers both to the spirits themselves and to living human initiates who have undergone the Kubandwa initiation and can be possessed by these spirits during ceremonies. The Kubandwa tradition represents one of the most sophisticated spirit-medium systems in African traditional religion
source: Sacred Texts - Myths and Legends of the Bantu; Wikipedia - Imana; HistoryWithIrebe substack

name: Kiranga
description: Kiranga is the central figure of the Kubandwa spirit possession cult in Burundi, a revered hero-spirit who bridges the gap between the supreme creator Imana and humanity. According to tradition, Kiranga was originally a mortal prince and accomplished hunter who met a tragic end when he was killed by a wounded antelope during a hunt. Far from simply passing into oblivion, his death transformed him into a powerful spirit who became the leader of the imandwa, the company of hero-spirits who serve as intermediaries between the divine and mortal realms. The Kubandwa cult, which worships Kiranga, is one of the most important spiritual traditions in the Great Lakes region of Africa, incorporating elements of ancestor veneration, spirit mediumship, and therapeutic ritual. Kiranga role is essential for maintaining cosmic order, allowing humans to communicate with Imana and receive divine assistance for healing, fertility, and protection
source: Springer Nature - Kiranga Cult; Wikipedia - Imana; HistoryWithIrebe - Mysticism in Old Rwanda; Sacred Texts - Bantu mythology

name: Bwiti
description: Bwiti is a complex spiritual discipline from Gabon and surrounding regions of Central Africa, centered on the ritual use of iboga (Tabernanthe iboga), a psychoactive plant root that induces profound visionary states. As one of Gabon's three official religions alongside Christianity and Islam, Bwiti represents a sophisticated system of spiritual knowledge, healing practices, and cosmological understanding that has survived centuries of colonial disruption. The Bwiti tradition involves elaborate initiation ceremonies lasting several days, during which initiates consume iboga under the guidance of experienced practitioners called Nganga. These ceremonies are designed to facilitate direct contact with ancestral spirits, reveal the root causes of illness or misfortune, and provide transformative spiritual insights that reshape the initiate's understanding of existence
source: Gabonese Bwiti religion — spirit documented in Gabonese spiritual tradition.

name: Bynesånden
description: Bynesånden (the Byneset Spirit) is a local ghost from the Byneset area of Trondheim, a rural district on the west side of the Trondheimsfjord. The spirit is believed to be the ghost of a woman who died of a broken heart after her lover was lost at sea. She is said to appear at the Byneset church (one of the oldest stone churches in Norway, dating to around 1180) and along the Byneset shoreline. The Bynesånden appears as a woman in traditional Norwegian folk dress, walking silently along the road or standing at the churchyard gate, waiting for her lost love to return. She is considered a gentle ghost — she does not frighten people deliberately but is a melancholy presence. Some versions say she appears before major storms to warn fishermen not to go out. The legend is recorded in the Norsk Folkeminnesamling's archives from Byneset, confirming it as an established part of local Trøndelag folklore
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Cadejo
description: Cadejo is a spirit from Central American mythology. The legend has pre-Columbian indigenous origins, where dogs were believed to help humans pass into the afterlife. With the arrival of Christianity, the story evolved into a dualistic tale. The White Cadejo, with blue eyes, is a protective spirit that guards drunkards, lost travelers, and innocent children from harm. The Black Cadejo, with burning red eyes, is a malevolent entity that preys on evildoers, drunks, and those with impure intentions — stalking them through village streets and stealing their souls. The Salvadoran writer Manlio Argueta immortalized these creatures in his children's book 'Magic Dogs of the Volcanoes' (Los Perros Mágicos de Los Volcanes). The Cadejo legend is so important that Salvadorans dress up as the dogs in Independence Day parades
source: Belizean oral tradition; snip LegendsofBelize.com; snip GrisDismation

name: Cadejo
description: El Cadejo is a legendary spirit from Salvadoran folklore that manifests as two spectral dogs — a White Cadejo and a Black Cadejo — representing the eternal struggle between good and evil. The legend has pre-Columbian indigenous origins, where dogs were believed to help humans pass into the afterlife. With the arrival of Christianity, the story evolved into a dualistic tale. The White Cadejo, with blue eyes, is a protective spirit that guards drunkards, lost travelers, and innocent children from harm. The Black Cadejo, with burning red eyes, is a malevolent entity that preys on evildoers, drunks, and those with impure intentions — stalking them through village streets and stealing their souls. The Salvadoran writer Manlio Argueta immortalized these creatures in his children's book 'Magic Dogs of the Volcanoes' (Los Perros Mágicos de Los Volcanes). The Cadejo legend is so important that Salvadorans dress up as the dogs in Independence Day parades
source: Mesoamerican mythology, Popol Vuh & Florentine Codex

name: Čáhcerávga
description: Čáhcerávga (Water Wraith) is a fictional creature in Sami folklore, explicitly known to be invented to scare children away from dangerous waters. Unlike the Rávga, which was believed to be a real undead spirit, the Čáhcerávga was recognized as a pedagogical tool. It was described as a long-necked, scary creature that could carry a child away if they went too close to the water. It was said to appear in all bodies of water where children were not supposed to go — lakes, rivers, ponds, and even wells. This belief shows how Sami folklore functioned as practical safety education in the Arctic landscape, where drowning in ice-cold water was a real and constant danger for children. The near-freezing waters of Sapmi meant that falling in could be fatal within minutes, making such scare-stories a matter of survival
source: saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; Qvigstad collection

name: Camazotz
description: Camazotz (meaning 'Death Bat' in K'iche' Maya) is a bat spirit and death god in Late Post-Classic Maya mythology from the Popol Vuh. He serves the lords of the underworld, Xibalba. In the Maya Hero Twins myth, Camazotz appears in the 'House of Bats' trial, where Hunahpu and Xbalanque must spend the night surrounded by circling bats. When Hunahpu sticks his head out of his blowgun to check if the sun has risen, Camazotz immediately snatches off his head and carries it to the ballcourt to be used as a ball by the death gods. In Classic Maya iconography, the leaf-nosed bat is depicted as a person's nahual or way-spirit bringing disease over enemies. The bat is associated with night, death, and sacrifice throughout Mesoamerica. Camazotz remains one of the most recognizable figures from the Popol Vuh and has appeared in popular culture including Dungeons & snip Dragons, Stranger Things, the Monsterverse graphic novels, and Fate/Grand Order
source: Maya mythology; Camazotz is the bat god associated with night and death.

name: Cannibal Giants
description: Cannibal Giants are fearsome creatures from the oral traditions of various First Nations peoples across Canada, particularly among the Algonquian and Athabaskan-speaking tribes of the Subarctic and northern woodlands. Known by different names in different languages, these beings share a common archetype: giant humanoid monsters driven by an insatiable hunger for human flesh that embody the harsh and unforgiving nature of the northern wilderness. Unlike the spirits and animal guides that feature prominently in many Indigenous traditions, these giants are unequivocally malevolent, representing the dangers that await those who venture alone into the deep forest or who violate the sacred balance between humans and the natural world In Canada folklore, this figure is known among the Canada people.
source: Pacific Northwest indigenous folklore — cannibal giants documented in Kwakwaka'wakw and related oral tradition.

name: Canyon People
description: The Canyon People are enigmatic spirit beings from Apache traditional narratives, particularly associated with the dramatic canyon landscapes of the American Southwest. In Apache cosmology, these beings inhabit the deep gorges, cliff walls, and hidden alcoves that characterize the region, serving as guardians of sacred places and intermediaries between the human world and the spirit realm. Unlike malevolent entities, the Canyon People are complex figures that can be either helpful or dangerous depending on how they are approached and whether proper respect is shown. They are part of a rich tradition of place-based spirits that reflect the deep connection between Apache people and their ancestral lands, where every geographical feature holds spiritual significance and is inhabited by unseen beings
source: Apache spiritual tradition; documented in Southwestern ethnographic records.

name: Capelobo
description: Capelobo is a therianthropic vampire-like monster from Brazilian mythology, particularly prevalent in the northern states of Pará and Maranhão. Its name fuses the Guarani word capê, meaning broken or crooked leg, with the Portuguese lobo, meaning wolf, describing both its appearance and its lupine nature. The Capelobo is closely related to other Brazilian monsters such as the Mapinguari and the Lobisomem, representing a distinct regional variant of the werewolf archetype that incorporates elements of Amazonian wildlife. Unlike European werewolves that are typically humans who transform into wolves, the Capelobo is a permanent monster that takes features from local animals including the tapir, peccary, and giant anteater, making it a uniquely Brazilian adaptation of the shapeshifter legend deeply rooted in indigenous folklore
source: Brazilian Amazon folklore — Capelobo werewolf-like cryptid documented by Câmara Cascudo.

name: Carival
description: Carival is a spirit of celebration and excess from Trinidadian and Tobagonian folklore, embodying the wild, transformative energy of Carnival. Unlike most traditional spirits that haunt specific locations or prey on the unwary, Carival is a seasonal entity that awakens during the Carnival season, possessing participants with an irresistible urge to dance, sing, and lose themselves in the festivities. This spirit reflects the unique cultural fusion of Trinidad and Tobago, where African, European, and indigenous Caribbean traditions blended to create one of the world's most famous Carnival celebrations. Carival represents the liminal space between ordinary life and the temporary madness of Carnival, where social rules are suspended, identities are masked, and the spirit of revelry takes control
source: Trinidadian folklore — spirit documented in Trinidadian oral tradition.

name: Cat Sídhe
description: The Cat Sídhe, also known as Cat-sìth in Scottish Gaelic, is a fairy creature from Celtic mythology that resembles a large spectral black cat with a distinctive white spot on its chest. This being spans both Scottish and Irish folklore, though it is more prominent in Scottish Highland traditions. Unlike ordinary fairy creatures, the Cat Sídhe occupies an ambiguous space between fairy, witch, and omen of death, reflecting the complex relationship between the Celtic otherworld and the mundane realm. The legend may have been inspired by actual encounters with the Scottish wildcat, which is larger and more ferocious than domestic cats, or by the Kellas cat, a hybrid between wildcats and domestic cats found only in Scotland. The Cat Sídhe is one of several supernatural felines in Celtic lore, alongside the Cù-sìth (fairy dog) and the Ceffyl Dŵr (water horse)
source: Celtic mythology, Irish Mythological Cycle & Mabinogion

name: Cemi (Taino Spirit Being and Sacred Object)
description: Cemi (also spelled Zemi) refers to both the spirit beings in Taino mythology and the sacred objects that housed them. In Taino belief, the world was populated by countless zemis -- spirits that inhabited natural features (mountains, rivers, caves, trees) and could be invoked through carved stone, wood, shell, or bone objects. The most distinctive form of zemi is the three-pointed stone (trigonolito), usually carved from limestone or guayacan wood, representing the connection between the three layers of the Taino universe: the heavens (turei), the earth, and the watery underworld (coaybay). Major zemis included Yocahu (supreme god), Atabey (mother goddess), Guabancex (goddess of chaos), and Baibrama (god of cassava). Chief zemis were kept in sacred houses (bohio del cemi) and consulted for divination using the cohoba ritual -- an inhalation of hallucinogenic powder that allowed the behike (shaman-priest) to communicate with the spirits
source: Taino oral tradition, Puerto Rico folklore

name: Changó
description: Changó, also spelled Shangó or Xangô, is one of the most powerful and revered orishas in the Yoruba religion and its Afro-Caribbean derivatives including Santería, Candomblé, and Lukumí. As the orisha of thunder, lightning, fire, war, dance, and justice, Changó embodies masculine power, passion, and royal authority. Originally a historical king of the Oyo Empire in what is now Nigeria, he was deified after death and became the第四 king of the Yoruba pantheon. During the transatlantic slave trade, his worship was carried to Cuba, Brazil, Trinidad, and other parts of the Americas, where he was syncretized with Saint Barbara in Catholic tradition due to the shared symbolism of lightning and thunder. Changó remains one of the most widely worshipped orishas in the Afro-American diaspora, representing the indomitable spirit of resistance and the power of righteous anger
source: Santería religion — Changó/Shango is the thunder deity documented in Afro-Caribbean religious tradition.

name: Chang Er
description: Chang'e, also originally known as Heng'e, is the revered Chinese goddess of the Moon and one of the most prominent figures in Chinese mythology, folk religion, and cultural tradition. Her story is intimately connected with the myth of Hou Yi, the legendary archer who shot down nine of the ten suns that once scorched the earth. According to the ancient divination text Guicang from the Zhou Dynasty, Chang'e ascended to the Moon after consuming an elixir of immortality. Over millennia, her story has evolved through countless poems, paintings, and festivals, making her a symbol of nostalgia, solitude, feminine beauty, and the eternal human longing for the unreachable. She is celebrated annually during the Mid-Autumn Festival, one of the most important holidays in Chinese culture, when families gather under the full moon to eat mooncakes and honor her myth
source: Chinese mythology; the moon goddess Chang'e.

name: Chang Pheuak (White Elephant)
description: The White Elephant (Thai: ช้างเผือก, chang pheuak) is the most sacred animal in Thai mythology and a direct symbol of royal power connected to Buddhist cosmology. According to legend, Queen Maya, the mother of the Buddha, dreamt of a white elephant offering her a lotus flower before she conceived — establishing the white elephant as a symbol of spiritual purity and royal legitimacy. The discovery of a white elephant was considered a divine sign that the reigning king ruled with righteousness (dharma). The legend of Phra Phutthabat (the Buddha's footprint) tells of a white elephant that knelt to show the sacred footprint at Saraburi province. White elephants were so revered they received royal titles, were never forced to work, and were considered members of the royal family. The Thai national flag historically featured a white elephant on a red background
source: Thai royal chronicles, Buddhist Jataka tales, Thai folklore

name: Charonda
description: Charonda is a type of vampire-like creature from Cypriot folklore, representing the island's unique blend of Greek, Byzantine, and Near Eastern supernatural traditions. The name likely derives from Charon, the ferryman of Hades in Greek mythology, connecting these beings to the realm of the dead and the concept of souls that cannot find rest. In Cypriot folk belief, Charondes are the restless spirits of individuals who led sinful lives, died unbaptized, or were not given proper burial rites, condemned to wander the earth as blood-drinking entities that prey on the living. This figure shares characteristics with the Greek vrykolakas and the Balkan vampire traditions, adapted to the specific cultural and religious landscape of Cyprus where Orthodox Christian beliefs merged with ancient pagan superstitions
source: Cypriot folklore — vampire documented in Cypriot oral tradition.

name: Chase Vault
description: The Chase Vault mystery is one of the most famous and enduring paranormal legends of the Caribbean, centered on a family tomb in the Christ Church cemetery of Barbados. Between 1812 and 1820, the heavy lead-lined coffins interred in the Chase family vault were repeatedly found disturbed, moved from their original positions, and in some cases overturned, despite the vault being sealed with a marble slab and showing no signs of forced entry. This bizarre phenomenon attracted widespread attention, including official investigations by colonial authorities including Lord Combermere, the Governor of Barbados. The mystery has inspired countless theories ranging from natural causes like flooding and earthquake tremors to supernatural explanations involving spirits, curses, and malevolent entities, making it one of the most famous haunted vault cases in paranormal history
source: Barbadian folklore — the Chase Vault mystery documented in Barbadian oral tradition.

name: Cheval Mal Fet
description: Cheval Mal Fet, meaning wicked horse in Haitian Creole, is a malevolent phantom horse from the folklore of Haiti and the French Caribbean. This spectral steed is deeply rooted in Haitian Vodou traditions and the colonial history of Saint-Domingue. The Cheval Mal Fet haunts the dense forests and misty mountains of Haiti, particularly the Massif de la Hotte and the Artibonite Valley. According to legend, the creature manifests from the restless spirits of horses that died in battle, torture, or neglect during the brutal plantation era, carrying the accumulated suffering and rage of centuries. Encounters with the Cheval Mal Fet are considered omens of imminent death or catastrophic misfortune, and its appearance is said to foretell violent storms, earthquakes, or the death of a community leader
source: Belgian folklore — ghost horse documented in Belgian Walloon oral tradition.

name: Chhinnamasta (Self-Decapitated Goddess)
description: Chhinnamasta ('the Self-Decapitated One') is a powerful Tantric goddess, one of the ten Mahavidyas (great wisdom goddesses) in Shaktism. The legend tells that once, while bathing in the Mandakini River with her attendants Dakini and Varnini, Parvati (in her form as Chhinnamasta) was overcome by a ravenous hunger that her attendants also felt. When asked to satisfy their hunger, Parvati severed her own head with a sword and held it in her hand. Three jets of blood spurted from her severed neck — one feeding her own mouth, and two feeding her attendants. The iconography shows her standing in a battlefield or cremation ground, holding her severed head, drinking her own blood. Her name literally means 'she whose head is severed.' The myth symbolizes the goddess's power to transcend death and her role as both destroyer and sustainer of cosmic energy (Shakti). Chhinnamasta represents the realization that the true self is beyond the body, and that life and death are two aspects of the same divine reality. She is associated with self-sacrifice, spiritual awakening, and the transcendence of ego
source: Tantric Shakta traditions, Mahavidya texts, Bengali Hindu folklore

name: Chichkhan
description: Chichkhan is a diminutive mountain dwarf from Kazakh and broader Central Asian Turkic folklore, known to inhabit remote caves and rocky crevices of the Tien Shan and Altai mountain ranges. These reclusive beings are part of the rich animistic tradition of the Kazakh people, where natural features like mountains, rivers, and caves were believed to house various spirits. The Chichkhan is associated with the concept of yer-su, or earth-water spirits, that protect specific geographical locations. Stories of Chichkhan have been passed down through oral tradition among Kazakh herders and mountaineers for centuries, serving as cautionary tales about respecting the natural world and the hidden dangers of venturing alone into treacherous mountain terrain where supernatural beings guard the earth's hidden treasures
source: Kazakh folklore — Chichkhan dwarf-like figure.

name: Chickcharney
description: The Chickcharney is a legendary bird-like creature from the folklore of Andros Island in the Bahamas, one of the most distinctive mythological beings in Caribbean oral tradition. According to Bahamian legend, the Chickcharney inhabits the dense pine forests of Andros, the largest island in the Bahamas archipelago. The creature has been part of local folklore for centuries, with stories passed down through generations. A notable legend connects the Chickcharney to Neville Chamberlain, the former British Prime Minister, who allegedly angered Chickcharnies by cutting down their trees while working on a sisal plantation in the Bahamas, causing his political career to be cursed. Modern researchers, including paleontologist Lisa G. Buckley, suggest that the Chickcharney legend may be based on the prehistoric barn owl species Tyto pollens, which coexisted with ancient humans in the Bahamas
source: Bahamian folklore — the Chickcharney cryptid documented in Andros Island oral tradition.

name: Chickcharnies
description: Chickcharnies, a variant spelling of Chickcharney, are mischievous feathered spirits from the folklore of Andros Island in the Bahamas, deeply woven into Bahamian oral tradition. These creatures are considered omens of either great fortune or terrible misfortune, depending on how they are treated. The legend of the Chickcharnies is concentrated in the dense pine forests of Andros, where they are believed to be guardians of the natural order. The most famous story involving Chickcharnies concerns British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain, who worked on his father's sisal plantation on Andros in his youth. According to local legend, Chamberlain cut down trees inhabited by Chickcharnies, bringing a curse that doomed his political career and contributed to the failure of the Munich Agreement decades later, serving as a powerful cautionary tale about respecting nature
source: Bahamian folklore — the Chickcharney forest spirit documented in Andros Island oral tradition.

name: Chil-kuyz
description: Chil-kuyz is a cave spirit from Uzbek and broader Central Asian folklore, rooted in the pre-Islamic animistic traditions of the Turkic peoples of the region. The name translates approximately to spirit of the wilderness or wild place guardian in Uzbek. These spirits are associated with the network of caves, grottoes, and underground springs found throughout the mountainous regions of Uzbekistan, particularly in the Nuratau and Zarafshan ranges. Chil-kuyz are part of a broader class of yer-su (earth-water) spirits venerated by Central Asian peoples since ancient times, maintaining the balance between the human world and the hidden realms beneath the earth. Local communities traditionally offered small tributes before entering caves believed to be inhabited by these spirits, reflecting the deep respect for the unseen forces of the natural world
source: Uzbek folklore — Chil Kuyz nature spirit.

name: Chindi
description: Chindi (Navajo: ch'ijidii) is a concept in Navajo religious belief referring to the negative spiritual residue left behind after a person dies. Unlike a ghost in the Western sense, the Chindi is not the soul of the deceased but an accumulation of everything negative about their life including pain, fear, anger, disappointment, resentment, and rejection. According to Navajo tradition, the Chindi leaves the body with the person's last breath and lingers in the vicinity of the death site and the deceased's possessions. Traditional Navajo practices surrounding death are deeply shaped by the need to manage, disperse, or avoid contact with the Chindi, which is believed to cause illness, misfortune, and even death. The concept reflects the Navajo emphasis on harmony and balance known as hozho, where negative energy must be carefully managed to maintain spiritual health
source: Navajo (Diné) spiritual tradition; documented in Southwestern ethnographic records.

name: Chitapo (Lake Spirit)
description: Chitapo (also spelled Kitapo) is a female lake spirit from the mythology of the Lamba and Bemba people of Zambia. She resides at the bottom of lakes, where she hoards vast treasures of diamonds and emeralds. Chitapo is a malicious spirit who lures people to a watery grave, not unlike sirens and mermaids in European legends. She is sometimes described as a mermaid, with the upper body of an attractive woman and the lower body of a fish. However, this mermaid-like imagery may have resulted from conflation with the Funkwe, a giant water snake with the tail of a fish that is said to inhabit the same lakes and serve as Chitapo's guardian. In some variations, the lake spirit takes the form of a small diamond that sits in the mouth of the giant snake, protecting it. Chitapo is also associated with children born under ill omens, whom she is said to dispose of. Lakes Nakamwale, Kashiba, and Namulolobwe in Zambia are particularly associated with the Chitapo legend. Offerings are sometimes made to appease her before fishing or swimming
source: bestiarium (Tumblr); Zambian oral traditions

name: Chiuta (The Spider Creator)
description: Chiuta, meaning 'Great Bow' (a reference to the rainbow as his symbol), is the supreme creator deity in Chewa and Tumbuka mythology of Malawi. Unlike many creator gods who are remote and uninvolved, Chiuta is depicted as intimately connected to creation through the powerful image of a spider descending from the sky on a silk thread. According to the Chewa creation myth, in the beginning there was only Chiuta and the barren earth. Chiuta lived above in the sky, and below him the earth was desolate. One day, clouds began to cover the sky, lightning flared, and thunder rumbled. The sky opened, and Chiuta, in the form of a spider, descended on a silk thread from the heavens to the earth, bringing life and fertility. The rainbow is considered Chiuta's visible manifestation, bridging the heavens and the earth. Chiuta is omnipresent but shapeless, and while prayers can be made directly to him, ancestors and spirits play a large intermediary role. The deity is associated with natural phenomena from the sky, such as rain and thunderstorms
source: Wikipedia (Tumbuka mythology); Chewa oral traditions; adonarhudo.wordpress.com

name: Cholula
description: Cholula is a figure from Mexican folklore particularly associated with the state of Puebla and the region around the Great Pyramid of Cholula. This legendary giant is part of a rich tradition of giants and trickster figures in Mexican mythology that predates the Spanish conquest and evolved through the colonial period. According to folk tradition, Cholula was a giant who inhabited the area before humans arrived, and the massive pyramid of Tlachihualtepetl, the largest pyramid by volume in the world, was built by or around him. The Cholula legend combines pre-Hispanic Nahua mythology with Spanish colonial influences, creating a unique folkloric figure representing the blending of two cultures. The giant is depicted in local festivals and stories as both a comedic figure and a cautionary tale about the consequences of excessive behavior
source: Aztec/Mexica folklore — the giant of Cholula from Aztec oral tradition.

name: Chort
description: Chort is an anthropomorphic malevolent spirit or demon in Slavic folk tradition, found across Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Polish, Czech, Slovak, and other Slavic cultures. The term chort represents a complex figure that evolved from pre-Christian Slavic mythology into Christian folk demonology. In Slavic paganism, chort was associated with Chernobog, the god of darkness, and considered a son of the dark deity and the goddess Mara. With Christianization, the chort was syncretized with the Christian devil. However, in many folk traditions, particularly Ukrainian and Czech, the chort retained a distinct identity as a trickster and tempter rather than an embodiment of absolute evil, often portrayed as surprisingly foolish and easily outwitted by clever peasants who manage to turn the demon's own schemes against him
source: Ukrainian folklore — Chort is a demon documented in Ukrainian and East Slavic oral tradition.

name: Chullachaqui
description: Chullachaqui, also known as Shapishico, is a mythical forest creature from the Peruvian and Brazilian Amazon jungle, prominent in the folklore of the Quechua, Shipibo, and other indigenous peoples of the Amazon Basin. The name derives from the Quechua words chulla meaning one or odd and chaki meaning foot, referring to the creature's most distinctive physical trait of mismatched feet. The Chullachaqui is a guardian spirit of the rainforest, protector of trees and animals, and punisher of those who break taboos in the forest. According to Amazonian tradition, the Chullachaqui belongs to an older species that lived in the rainforest long before humans. Most of the time these beings dwell in remote forest spots far from human habitation where they tend their own gardens, uninterested in human affairs
source: Amazonian Quechua folklore — the Chullachaqui shapeshifting forest spirit.
